stories.summary: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 2 – A… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Long Cloud on Mars Explanation: What’s causing this unusually long cloud on Mars ? Known as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC) and first recorded by NASA’s Viking Orbiter 2 in 1977, the strange cloud has been imaged in greater detail more recently by ESA ’s robotic Mars Express spacecraft. The featured image is from 2018. The cloud forms only during spring and summer seasons and then only during morning hours. Made of water-ice, the most familiar process that causes cloud crystals to form around bits of dust would fail due to the thinness and lack of dust high in the Martian atmosphere . Leading speculation holds that dust is not involved. After the cloud forms near the volcano Arsia Mons , wind blows the cloud downstream — creating a tail that can extend over 1500 kilometers. Efforts to better understand AMEC s will continue, an understanding that may bolster a more complete view of cloud formation on Earth . stories.title: Pennsylvania’s Grand Canyon
stories.summary: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Pennsylvania’s Grand Canyon Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search October 25, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison North-central Pennsylvania is canyon country with an Appalachian flair. Pine Creek Gorge reaches depths of about 1,500 feet (460 meters) along its gently curving path through the forests of the Allegheny Plateau . Instead of the steep rock walls characteristic of canyons in the desert Southwest, lushly vegetated slopes outline the dramatic topography. In autumn, greens give way to a palette of reds and golds sought out by leaf peepers. Nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of Pennsylvania,” the gorge runs for some 45 miles (72 kilometers) from Ansonia south to Pine Creek’s confluence with the West Branch Susquehanna River, reaching its greatest depths around Waterville. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 8 satellite captured this image of Pine Creek Gorge on October 25, 2026, when colorful fall foliage was on display. Glaciers played a key role in the canyon’s formation, though ice itself did not carve it. Pine Creek once flowed to the north , opposite of what it does today. As glaciers advanced into the region from the northeast during the last ice age, they dammed the river and filled the valley with lakes. Those lakes eventually overflowed, sending water streaming to the south. Autumn colors emerge along Pine Creek Gorge in this view from Colton Point State Park on October 11, 2009. fishhawk , via Flickr When the ice receded, Pine Creek was already becoming entrenched in its southward course. Rocks and sand left behind by the melting ice further prevented the water from turning back north. Glacial meltwater continued to rush through the valley, deepening and shaping it into its current form. Today, the hillsides around the gorge are blanketed in northern hardwood and mixed oak forest, sprinkled with hemlock and white pine. In autumn, the deciduous trees impart red and gold hues to the landscape akin to the rock of the famous Arizona canyon . October 9 October 25 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison October 9 October 25 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison October 9 October 25 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Image Details Foliage in the northern hardwood and oak forests around Pennsylvania’s Pine Creek Gorge takes on fall color between October 9, 2026 (left), and October 25, 2026 (right). The images were acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 . NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison. This seasonal change around Pine Creek Gorge has not always been so visually pleasing. With increasing demand for wood products in early 19th-century America, loggers found their way to the area’s stately trees. At the time, white pine and hemlock several feet in diameter and towering hardwoods populated the slopes around Pine Creek Gorge. The pines were especially valued for making ship masts, and hemlock bark was used to tan leather. Before railroads, logs were floated down Pine Creek to the Susquehanna in massive drives. By the early 20th century, decades of logging left the land so barren that the area earned the moniker “Pennsylvania Desert.” The forest has since returned, and with it, wild inhabitants such as black bears, coyotes, bobcats, timber rattlesnakes, and a diversity of songbirds. In 1968, an area of 30,000 acres (12,000 hectares) was designated a National Natural Landmark . Visitors can experience the gorge’s natural splendor at many points along its path, including from multiple state parks and the Pine Creek Rail Trail . Through multiple park experiences at MAX POWER , NASA and a variety of external collaborators will showcase the newest aircraft, autonomous vehicles, technologies, and more defining the future of air and space. NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 plane, and agency partners will showcase Moon rovers, spacecraft, and more. The expo also is a culmination of the agency’s recent Inspiration Tour , which included numerous flyovers to highlight NASA’s fleet of aircraft. A current schedule of events is available on the agency’s website . MAX POWER includes opportunities to meet leadership, astronauts, engineers, scientists, and other subject matter experts during the family-friendly public events with gates opening at 9 a.m. EST on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8. NASA also will share multiple news updates during the weekend, including hosting a news conference at 5 p.m. on Nov. 7, to provide its latest Moon Base update. Located near the lunar South Pole, the Moon Base is humanity’s first outpost for long-term lunar exploration. Live coverage of the news conference will stream on a variety of platforms online. stories.title: Space Crops and Advanced Tech Wrap Up Week Following Spacewalk
stories.summary: Expedition 75 flight engineers Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) and Jessica Watkins of NASA pose together inside the International Space Station’s Quest airlock during a spacesuit fit check. NASA/Anil Menon Space crops research wrapped up the week following the completion of the first of two power upgrade spacewalks at the International Space Station . The Expedition 75 crew members rounded out their research schedule with virtual reality and super intelligence studies. The orbital outpost has a new roll-out solar array that is generating power after flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) installed it during a spacewalk on Thursday . Menon and Kutryk spent seven hours and 11 minutes in the vacuum of space attaching the roll-out solar array to the port side truss structure then releasing its tension bolts allowing the solar array to unfurl, or roll out, on its own during a ten-minute process. The pair will install one more roll-out solar array on Thursday, Nov. 5, to complete the yearslong process that began in June 2021 to augment the space station’s power generation system. Menon and Kutryk will install the eighth and final roll-out solar array on the starboard side of the truss structure increasing the station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts. Menon and Kutryk had a light duty day on Friday with ongoing research planned for their short schedule. Menon worked on a space botany investigation in the Kibo laboratory module exploring how microgravity affects cell division on green algae and cultured tobacco cells. Results may support the production of food crops on the Moon and Mars. Kutryk pedaled on the European Enhanced Exploration Exercise Device’s (E4D) exercise cycle in the Columbus laboratory module . The compact all-in-one E4D is being tested for its ability to keep crews fit during a long-term spaceflight. NASA flight engineer Luke Delaney also studied space-based crops focusing on how to prevent plant diseases in microgravity. Delaney inoculated thale cress plant samples after they were exposed to a fungal pathogen then stowed the samples inside an artificial gravity-generating incubator . Results may improve crop disease resistance both on Earth and in space. NASA flight engineer Jessica Watkins spent her shift servicing a variety of research hardware. She first removed and photographed components inside a device that powers experiments launched aboard spacecraft. Next, Watkins swapped moisture absorbers inside a set of portable science freezers that can be launched to the station and returned back to Earth housing frozen research samples for analysis. Station commander Pyotr Dubrov of Roscosmos worked on a physics experiment swapping hardware inside a temperature-controlled chamber to explore manufacturing high-purity semiconductor crystals in microgravity. Flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov wore a virtual reality headset and responded to computerized visual stimuli to testing how his sense of balance and orientation is adapting to microgravity. Flight engineer Anna Kikina studied how super intelligence tools may increase operational and communications efficiency aboard a spacecraft. stories.title: NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope
stories.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope returns to orbit as an improved telescope after its second servicing mission in February 1997. NASA NASA issued a Request for Information Oct. 29 to learn more about industry capabilities for in-space servicing to support the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope. “Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.” The Request for Information seeks commercial interest in: potentially conducting a mission to boost Hubble to a higher altitude to extend its science lifetime; servicing Hubble to enhance its capabilities; or performing a safe, controlled re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble’s mission. “Hubble is a national icon that has fundamentally changed how humanity views our universe for more than 35 years,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing. Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated re-entry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow.” The Request for Information is available online and will remain open for responses until 3 p.m. EST, Monday, Nov. 30. Like all spacecraft in low Earth orbit, Hubble’s altitude is slowly decreasing over time because of atmospheric drag. Hubble does not have a propulsion system to maintain its own orbit, and analysis predicts Hubble is likely to re-enter the atmosphere in the 2033 to 2034 timeframe. As such, NASA anticipates that a mission would need to take place by 2032. The Hubble Space Telescope has been operating for more than three decades and continues to make ground-breaking discoveries that shape our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency). NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, manages the telescope and mission operations. Lockheed Martin Space, based in Denver, also supports mission operations at Goddard. The Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, conducts Hubble science operations for NASA. stories.title: November’s Night Sky Notes: Light-Day Away
stories.summary: 2 min read November’s Night Sky Notes: Light-Day Away NASA’s Voyager mission took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. The twin spacecraft revealed details about Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune – using each planet’s gravity to send them on to the next destination. Voyager set the stage for such ambitious orbiter missions as Galileo to Jupiter and Cassini to Saturn. Today both Voyager spacecraft continue to return valuable science from the far reaches of our solar system. NASA/JPL-Caltech Twin Travelers In 1977, NASA launched twin spacecraft Voyager 1 and 2, taking advantage of a once-every-175-year planetary alignment of the four largest planets in our solar system: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Using six gravity assists between them, this Grand Tour gave us up-close views of the gas and ice giants, including several moons. By the 1980s, the two probes went their separate ways at Saturn. As Voyager 2 continued toward Uranus and Neptune, Voyager 1 grabbed one more portrait of the solar system (excluding Mercury and Mars), including a final image of the pale blue dot we call home. The Golden Record Cover NASA/JPL-Caltech Playlist “Hello from the children of planet Earth.” Every good road trip needs some music to match. In this case, each craft carries the Golden Record , a 12-inch phonograph record with spoken greetings in 55 languages, 27 musical tracks, 116 images, and other sounds from Earth. Each record is protected by an outer cover featuring etchings showing our Sun’s location relative to 14 pulsars, along with instructions on how to play it. The design used various metals to protect the information encoded from space radiation: the record used copper and gold plating, and the cover used aluminum. The cover was electroplated with an ultra-pure sample of the isotope uranium-238. Uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.468 billion years. Are We There Yet? Did you know that a light-minute is a measure of distance, not time? In August 2012 and November 2018, Voyager 1 and 2 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun’s solar wind meets the interstellar medium. Using NASA’s Deep Space Network , Earth communicates with both spacecraft and tracks each on its journey. At the time of this article, the Canberra antenna tracked Voyager 1 at 25.80 billion km, or just over 16 billion miles. This graphic shows the position of NASA’s Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes, outside of the heliosphere, a protective bubble created by the Sun that extends well past the orbit of Pluto. NASA/JPL-Caltech On November 18, 2026, 49 years after its launch, Voyager 1 will cross the one-light-day mark, 16.1 billion miles from the Sun. You may have heard the term light-year in your favorite sci-fi movie or show, or when stargazing and referring to an object outside of our solar system. This video best demonstrates the different distances between the inner solar system, outer solar system, and beyond, using light measurements. Additionally, track each Voyager spacecraft here . You can get a real understanding of what a gravity assist might be like with our Gravity Assist activity and learn what it’s like to measure a “light minute” with our Measuring a Kid Minute activity guide!

NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin March 22, 2025 October 10, 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Shrouded in ice in the lonely Weddell Sea, Vega Island is an eerie sight to behold. On this speck of land east of the Antarctic Peninsula, ice, rock outcrops, and glacial moraines combine to create the appearance of a smirking skull in profile looking toward Devil Island. These images show Vega Island’s creepy countenance at the start of austral autumn (left) and in spring (right). They were acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.) A nunatak jutting out of the ice has the appearance of an eye socket, a lateral moraine forms a mouth, and Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier constitutes a jawbone. In the March 2025 image, a layer of snow coats the ice, which is typical of the region’s wettest month. That contrasts with the October 2026 image, when snow is absent from large areas and darker ice surfaces are visible. Above-average temperatures in winter 2026 —particularly in June —were partly responsible for so much bare ice in October , said glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College. The ice exposed on Vega and nearby islands indicates limited new snow accumulation over the winter, further reduced by sublimation and wind scouring, he said. “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.” The melt season ahead may also be more trick than treat. Bare ice is darker than snow and absorbs more solar energy, meaning that melting is poised to speed up as the days grow longer and warmer. “Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said. “When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.” October 10, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin The first comprehensive mapping of Vega Island’s ice was aided by Landsat imagery. In a study published in 1982 , scientists described the island’s four ice caps with protruding rocky cliffs and outlet glaciers. They leveraged early Landsat observations along with aerial photos and topographic maps to catalog 29 glaciers on Vega. Of those glaciers, Devil’s Bay Glacier has been closely monitored since the austral summer of 1998-1999, with researchers measuring an overall decline in its mass. Satellite images acquired in recent decades show ice loss from other glaciers on the island as well, with increased areas of exposed bedrock. Long before scientists began tracking its glaciers, Vega was a bright spot in a tale of terror born out of early exploration of the area. The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 set out to study the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife on and around the eastern Antarctic Peninsula. The party became split into three groups during their explorations, isolated for a winter in different locations. Adding to the horror, they lost their ship to the pack ice. Cape Well-met, as it would come to be known, off the “forehead” of the Vega Island skull, was the site of a happy reunion of two of the groups in spring 1903. Soon thereafter, an Argentinean expedition rescued the survivors of the ordeal. NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . stories.title: Spacewalkers Install Roll-Out Solar Array for Power Generation
stories.summary: NASA astronaut Anil Menon rides the Canadarm2 robotic arm to begin the installation of a roll-out solar array on the International Space Station’s port-side truss structure while orbiting 260 miles above Earth. NASA+ NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk concluded their spacewalk outside the International Space Station at 3:08 p.m. EDT. During the 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk, Menon and Kutryk installed and deployed an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station’s 2A electrical power channel. The array is the seventh IROSA installed on the station and will provide additional power to support critical operations, including a safe and controlled deorbit. Menon and Kutryk also completed several get-ahead tasks to prepare for a planned Thursday, Nov. 5 spacewalk, when they will install the eighth and final IROSA on the 3B power channel. NASA will provide live coverage beginning at 6:45 a.m. Learn how to watch: https://www.nasa.gov/live/ Following the Nov. 5 spacewalk, the roll-out solar arrays will be fully installed, completing the space station’s power system augmentation. Together, the eight arrays will increase available power by up to 30%, boosting the station’s power generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts. U.S. spacewalk 100 was Menon’s fourth and Kutryk’s first. It also was the 285th spacewalk in support of space station assembly, maintenance, and upgrades. stories.summary: From left, Astronauts Anil Menon of NASA and Josha Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) pose for pre-flght crew portraits at Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. NASA Mission managers have given the go for Thursday’s spacewalk to install a new roll-out solar array on the International Space Station ’s port-side truss structure. Expedition 75 flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) will set their spacesuits to battery power at 8 a.m. EDT signifying the start of their spacewalk for about six hours and 45 minutes of external maintenance. NASA+ begins its live spacewalk coverage at 6:30 a.m. On Thursday, the spacewalking duo will first unbolt the roll-out solar array from a temporary stowage platform. Next, Menon will carry the roll-out solar array to the truss worksite while riding the Canadarm2 robotic arm . Kutryk will the translate to the port truss worksite while tethered to the orbital outpost and join Menon to complete the installation job. Finally, mission controllers will remotely activate the roll-out solar array to begin generating power. Menon and Kutryk began their shift on Wednesday finalizing their spacewalk procedure reviews. Afterward, the pair inspected their spacesuits’ life support systems, communications gear, and other components ensuring their readiness for Thursday’s excursion. After lunchtime, Menon and Kutryk joined NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney for a final spacewalk conference with specialists on the ground. Watkins and Delaney also familiarized themselves with lighting conditions and camera locations on the outside of the space station in order to monitor the spacewalkers and operate the Canadarm2. Finally, all four astronauts gathered at the end of their shift for a conference with robotics engineers to discuss Canadarm2 operations planned for the spacewalk. Roscosmos’ three cosmonauts had a light duty day on Wednesday keeping up their science activities and familiarizing themselves with Thursday’s spacewalk operations. Station commander Pyotr Dubrov uninstalled multi-wavelength Earth photography gear that autonomously captured Pacific and Atlantic Ocean landmarks during the crew’s sleep shift. Flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov installed a different set of Earth imagery gear for another overnight session to photograph Pacific islands and South American glaciers, meanwhile, flight engineer Anna Kikina jogged on the Zvezda service module ’s treadmill to test her fitness in microgravity. The pair photographed the robotic hardware for inspection, wrapped it in protective covers to seal sensitive components, then loaded it inside a SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft for return to Earth in November. Watkins still had time to prepare a specialized camera with the ability to film the electrical activity of thunderstorms at up to 100,000 frames per second for upcoming research operations inside the Columbus laboratory module . stories.summary: City lights sparkle across the southern United States in this photograph from the International Space Station is it orbited above Florida. At right, is a set of the orbital outpost’s main solar arrays augmented by a smaller set of roll-out solar arrays. NASA Expedition 75 began the week gearing up for a spacewalk to upgrade the International Space Station ’s power generation system. Research into bioprinted blood vessels and relaxation techniques, as well cargo operations rounded out Monday’s schedule. Flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) will exit the Quest airlock at 8 a.m. EDT on Thursday to install one of two roll-out solar arrays on the orbital outpost’s port side truss structure. NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney will support the spacewalkers in and out of their spacesuits and assist the duo with the Canadarm2 robotic arm during the planned six-hour and 45-minute spacewalk. Live coverage of the spacewalk will begin on NASA+ starting at 6:30 a.m. The four astronauts joined each other on Monday and familiarized themselves with the Canadarm2 maneuvers necessary to support Thursday’s spacewalk. Menon and Kutryk will first release the roll-out solar array from an external pallet. Menon then will attach himself to the robotic arm, retrieve the roll-out solar array, then ride the Canadarm2 to the installation worksite. Kutryk will remain tethered to the truss structure, translate to the port truss worksite, and join Menon to complete the installation job. Afterward, mission controllers will activate the new roll-out solar array. Menon and Kutryk also checked out their emergency spacesuit jetpacks for fuel quantity, battery power, and thruster functionality. Watkins then assisted Kutryk ensuring spacesuit cooling and water systems were safely configured for Thursday’s spacewalk. Watkins and Menon also had time to work inside the SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft transferring supplies back and forth from the space station. Dragon docked autonomously to the Harmony module ’s space-facing port on Oct. 15 and is due to return to Earth in mid-November loaded with science and hardware for analysis. Delaney began his shift documenting his sleep patterns on a computer tablet for the RelaxPro investigation that is exploring how to improve stress reduction during a long duration spaceflight. Next, he treated and nourished bioprinted blood vessel tissues helping researchers take advantage of microgravity to create custom, individualized tissues for patients. Station commander Pyotr Dubrov and flight engineer Anna Kikina, both from Roscosmos, partnered together wearing arm, wrist, and finger cuffs to measure the responsiveness of the circulatory system to weightlessness. Flight engineer Sergey Teteryanikov continued studying how super intelligence tools may advance crew operations and communications with mission controllers. stories.title: Advanced Research, Spacewalk Preps End Week as NASA Announces Artemis Status
stories.summary: The full Moon is pictured just above Earth’s horizon from the International Space Station as it soared 260 miles above Mexico. NASA The Expedition 75 crew worked on a 3D bioprinter and a levitation furnace at the end of the week to advance health and high-temperature physics. Two astronauts are also preparing for a spacewalk at the International Space Station as NASA announces the status of upcoming Moon missions. NASA flight engineers Luke Delaney and Anil Menon were back on bioprinting duty continuing to convert vascular cell samples into newly printed blood vessels . Delaney set up the BioFabrication Facility for printing and Menon processed the engineered human tissues for nourishing and cultivation. Flight engineer Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) swapped sample hardware inside a specialized research furnace that levitates samples with an electric field and heats them with lasers. NASA flight engineer Jessica Watkins tested the operations of backup water quality-testing hardware and a gas-flow controller. All four astronauts gathered together after lunchtime for a spacewalk procedures conference with engineers on the ground. Menon and Kutryk will exit the Quest airlock on Thursday, Oct. 29, to install a roll-out solar array on the station’s truss structure. Watkins and Delaney also trained to operate the Canadarm2 robotic arm to assist the spacewalkers next week. The cosmonaut trio from Roscosmos with Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina, and Sergey Teterytatnikov, completed a plasma crystal study that explored the interaction of highly charged gases and microscopic particles. The trio also serviced radiation detection gear, explored super intelligence tools, and collected blood pressure measurements on Friday. The orbital outpost is critical in preparing for missions to the Moon and eventually, Mars. Now the agency is accelerating its effort to return crews to the lunar surface by 2028 . stories.title: Busy Station Day with Bioprinting, Spacesuit Check, Robotics, and Photography
stories.summary: NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins (center) assists Canadian Space Agency astronaut Josh Kutryk as he practices suiting up in a spacesuit in an International Space Station airlock simulator at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. NASA/Josh Valcarcel The Expedition 75 crew members had a busy day on Thursday bioprinting blood vessels and trying on a spacesuit aboard the International Space Station . The orbital residents also trained to use a pair of robotic arms and set up Earth photography sessions to round out the day in low Earth orbit. A bioprinter, also called the BioFabrication Facility located in the Columbus laboratory module , was in operation aboard the orbital outpost printing blood vessels using vascular cells. NASA flight engineer Luke Delaney kicked off the advanced research operations removing the cells from a science freezer, thawing them, then mixing the samples with a biological printing material. Afterward, he loaded the mixture into the bioprinter and powered on the device to begin the bioprinting process. NASA flight engineer Anil Menon wrapped up the session preserving and nourishing the newly printed blood vessel tissues inside the bioprinter for cultivation. Earlier, Menon joined fellow NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins and assisted flight engineer Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) in the Quest airlock as he tried on a spacesuit ensuring a good fit, comfort, and systems functionality. Spacesuit fit checks also account for body changes such as spinal elongation that take place in microgravity. Menon and Kutryk are scheduled to exit Quest together on Oct. 29 for a spacewalk to install a roll-out solar array on the station’s port-side truss structure. Delaney trained on a computer to operate the Canadarm2 robotic arm that he will command to assist the spacewalkers during their roll-out solar array installation job next week. He and Watkins will also help the spacewalkers in and out of their spacesuits and guide them during their planned six-hour and 45-minute excursion. Roscosmos flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov also conducted robotics training and practiced how to operate the European robotic arm attached to the Nauka science module . Afterward, Teteryatnikov installed and activated Earth observation gear to capture Asian and South American landmarks in visible and near-infrared wavelengths during the crew’s sleep shift. Roscosmos flight engineer Anna Kikina pointed a camera out a Zvezda service module window and photographed lakes in eastern Africa. Kikina also assisted Teteryatnikov during his Earth camera configuration activities. Station commander Pyotr Dubrov of Roscosmos began his shift on orbital plumbing duties inside the Zvezda. stories.title: Spacesuits, Lunar Agriculture, and Breathing Research Top Wednesday’s Schedule
stories.summary: NASA astronaut Anil Menon points his camera toward his spacesuit’s helmet visor and takes an out-of-this-world “space selfie” during a spacewalk on Aug. 25, 2026.. NASA/Anil Menon Spacesuit checks topped Wednesday’s task list aboard the International Space Station as two astronauts prepare for a spacewalk next week. The Expedition 75 crew members also kept up advanced microgravity research exploring space agriculture and the respiratory system midweek. Flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) are gearing up for the first of two spacewalks that will see the duo install a pair of roll-out solar arrays on the orbital outpost’s truss structure. The spacewalkers are scheduled to exit the Quest airlock on Oct. 29 and Nov. 5 to finalize the yearslong solar array installation work increasing the station’s power generation capability by up to 30 percent. NASA+ coverage begins at 6:30 a.m. EDT for the Thursday, Oct. 29, spacewalk scheduled to start at 8 a.m. Then on Thursday, Nov. 5, NASA+ coverage starts at 6:45 a.m. EST with the second spacewalk beginning at 8:10 a.m. Menon and Kutryk spent Wednesday in Quest organizing tools, inspecting tethers, and cleaning spacesuit helmets they will use during the external power upgrade job. Afterward, the duo outfitted a pair of spacesuits with communications gear, medical monitoring hardware, and other components ahead of a suit fit verification planned for Thursday. Spacesuit fit checks account for body changes that take place in microgravity, ensure astronaut comfort, and confirm systems functionality. NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney reviewed the procedures they will use to assist the astronauts in and out of their spacesuits during both spacewalks. The duo, along with Menon and Kutryk, also studied the spacewalking procedures necessary to maneuver outside the space station, retrieve the solar arrays, and install them. Menon on Wednesday still had time to process green algae and cultured tobacco cell samples for the Plant Cell Division investigation. The space botany study takes place in the Kibo laboratory module and explores how to grow crops on the lunar and Martian surface to feed future crews. Roscosmos cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina took turns wearing an acoustic sensor around their necks that recorded their rapid exhalation rate. The high-quality airway sound recordings will be sent down to Earth for analysis to learn how living in microgravity affects a crew member’s breathing. Dubrov later swapped electronics gear on an exercise cycle while Kikina reorganized cargo and docking hardware inside the Progress 96 cargo spacecraft . Roscosmos flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov spent the first half of his shift servicing life support and communications gear. After lunchtime, Teteryatnikov collected air samples to analyze the station’s breathing environment then conducted a computerized hearing test to wrap up his shift. stories.title: NASA Completes Artemis III Booster Stacking, Shares Status Update
stories.summary: Engineers with NASA’s Exploration Ground Systems completed integrating the aerodynamic nose cones onto the left and right forward assemblies on the twin SLS (Space Launch System) solid rocket boosters, finishing their stacking operations for Artemis III inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Each forward assembly contains an aerodynamic top, a forward skirt housing avionics, and frustum housing motors that allow the boosters to separate from the SLS core stage after launch. The twin solid boosters will help support the remaining rocket components and the Orion spacecraft during final assembly of the Artemis III rocket and provide more than 75 percent of the total SLS thrust during liftoff from NASA Kennedy’s Launch Pad 39B. NASA/Cory S Huston Progress on NASA’s Artemis III’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket continues at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, where teams have completed the integration of the final solid rocket booster motor segments onto the mobile launcher for the “short stack” configuration that will be used during a tanking test. Teams also completed installation of all four RS-25 engines on the SLS core stage. Teams now will install the systems tunnel that runs the length of the core stage and is used to route pyrotechnic cabling, a system of wiring that allows the single-use, quick disconnect for controlled movements during liftoff, on the massive stage. In the coming weeks, the stage will be integrated with the solid rocket boosters, completing the rocket’s “short stack” configuration. NASA will roll the short stack SLS rocket from the spaceport’s Vehicle Assembly Building to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test in the coming months, where the Artemis launch team will practice procedures and timelines for loading propellant. While at the pad, the Artemis III crew, NASA astronauts Randy Bresnick, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano, also will conduct a launch day rehearsal and emergency exit walkdown. This will include suiting up in astronaut crew quarters, driving to the launch pad, ascending the mobile launcher, and then walking through the exit route they would take in the unlikely event of an emergency during launch countdown. Additional hardware updates At Launch Pad 39B, teams continue the refurbishment of the flame deflector, which saw minimal damage after the Artemis II launch. The bricks on the flame trench itself were not affected by the launch due to ground support improvements informed by lessons learned after Artemis I in 2022. Teams are continuing to work through testing on the Orion spacecraft. Recently, engineers with ESA and Airbus inspected the solar array wings, which deliver power to the service module that provides propulsion, thermal control, and electrical power to the spacecraft, as well as air and water for the crew. Technicians extend and inspect one of the solar array wing panels that will attach the Orion service module for Artemis III inside the Neil A. Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building high bay at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. Each solar array panel, provided by the European Space Agency and built by Airbus, generates 11 kilowatts of power and spans about 63 feet to supply Orion’s power, propulsion, air, and water through low Earth Orbit. NASA/Amanda Stevenson At NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, the forward and aft rings were welded on the Artemis III spacer, completing the primary structure. The spacer will serve to represent upper stage dimensions during the mission. The dimensional checks are underway. Engineers also are converting two existing structural test articles, the Orion stage adapter and launch vehicle stage adapter, into flight-ready hardware. Exterior painting on the Orion stage adapter was recently completed at NASA Marshall, with cables and brackets to be installed soon. The launch vehicle stage adapter has undergone detailed inspection and preparation, with corrosion removal nearly complete, and nondestructive evaluation will begin this fall. Following that evaluation, technicians will apply conversion coating to the interior, prime and paint the exterior, and spray the cone-shaped adapter with thermal protection spray foam. The spacer and both adapters remain on track to ship to Kennedy early next year. Crew training continues The Artemis III crew has continued a variety of training activities to prepare for their mission. Recently, they completed lessons on the flywheel exercise device, practicing hardware setup, anticipated exercises, and equipment disassembly. This compact device, about the size of an extra-large shoe box, uses pulleys and a torque limiter to mimic a rowing machine, allowing aerobic, resistive, and rowing exercises with straps attached to either a bar or harness. Nutrition also is a key focus. At NASA’s Space Food Systems Laboratory in Houston, crew members sampled nearly 200 items on the menu to select their favorites for the mission, ensuring their health and performance are supported throughout. The Artemis III crew tasted various food items on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026, at NASA’s Space Food Systems Laboratory, to determine what they’ll eat on their mission in low Earth orbit. NASA/Helen Arase Vargas The crew concluded helicopter underwater egress training, practicing escape from a submerged, upside-down mock helicopter cabin in a controlled pool environment to prepare for potential off-nominal water crash-landings. Last week, members of the Artemis III crew traveled to San Diego to participate in recovery training with NASA and military partners, practicing water lifts by U.S. Navy helicopters. They completed several suited training activities in the Orion Crew Survival System Suits this week, preparing for post-insertion, deorbit procedures, and emergency responses. These activities included communication system checks, suit operations, emergency equipment handling, contingency drills, and cabin configuration with stowage, ensuring the crew is ready for any scenario that may arise. The Artemis III astronauts pose for a group photo on the front porch before conducting hoist training with U.S. Navy Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron (HSC) 23 and Explosive Ordnance Disposal Group (EODGRU) 1 in San Diego, California, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. In preparation for NASA’s Artemis III, NASA and the Department of War will conduct training evolutions to demonstrate and evaluate the processes, procedures, and hardware used in recovery operations for crewed lunar missions. US Navy/2nd Class August Clawson In September, the full Artemis III crew and backup astronauts visited Florida together for the first time since their crew announcement earlier this year. The astronauts visited their Orion spacecraft, saw the integrated solid rocket boosters on top of the mobile launcher, and viewed the core stage undergoing final processing ahead of integration. The crew also visited commercial partners SpaceX and Blue Origin to become more oriented with the lunar lander providers’ progress, marking one more milestone in preparation for the daring Artemis III mission. For more information on the mission, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-iii/

stories.title: NASA Releases Artemis II Lunar Science Data, Images
stories.summary: NASA astronauts Christina Koch (below) and Victor Glover (above) share a window inside the Orion spacecraft during the sixth day of the Artemis II mission. Flight Day 6 was the crew’s lunar flyby day, during which they rotated roles taking photos, making annotations, and recording their scientific observations of the lunar surface. (April 6, 2026) NASA NASA’s Artemis II crew traveled around the Moon and back and, along the way, captured stunning imagery and scientific observations of our nearest neighbor. NASA is making the full lunar science dataset from their journey available Wednesday to the global science community and the public for further study. More than 800 gigabytes of Artemis II lunar science data – some previously unreleased – have been uploaded to NASA’s Planetary Data System, the public archive for NASA’s planetary missions. This data release includes more than 11,000 full-resolution images and video of the Moon from the crew’s handheld cameras and the Orion spacecraft’s cameras, 8.5 hours of audio recordings of the crew’s scientific observations of the lunar surface, and crew-annotated images. When combined, the images, audio files, and crew notes from the expedition provide a powerful lunar science dataset ripe for exploration and analysis. This is the first planetary science dataset captured primarily by humans in more than half a century and humanity’s influence on it is clear. Through training in classrooms, simulations, and field environments, NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen developed expertise in lunar geography, geology, and observational best practices. Their quick decisions about observation targets and which images to capture, along with their perceptions of color and dynamic changes, and discussions about the science of the lunar surface and its surroundings complement decades of data from Apollo astronauts and robotic explorers and deepen our understanding of the Moon as NASA prepares for long-term exploration of the lunar surface. A screenshot from an Artemis II crew member’s tablet shows handwritten annotations made during the lunar flyby on April 6, 2026, atop a visualization of the dark Moon eclipsing the Sun. Three crew members, who signed their first names, noted impact flashes and their locations on the image. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Victor “Ike” Glover wrote in blue and green, respectively, while CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen wrote in red. (April 7, 2026) NASA/CSA Along with this data, NASA has released the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report , the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report , and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide . Together, these three publications provide an overview of the Artemis II lunar mission data and activities, and a technical summary of how the science plan was developed and implemented. This information is already helping inform NASA’s exploration plans for Artemis III and beyond.
